questions.question: Design an ATM system. What are the key classes and interactions?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can decompose a real-world system into cohesive classes with clear responsibilities and model state transitions properly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting all logic in one ATM class instead of separating hardware components, state management, and business rules into distinct objects
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention explicit state machine design upfront and explain why external bank communication is abstracted through BankServer interface for testability

questions.direct_answer: An ATM system has core classes: ATM (Singleton controller), Card, Account, BankServer (external verification), CashDispenser (manages denominations), CardReader, and ATMState hierarchy (State pattern). The ATM flows through states: Idle → CardInserted → Authenticated → SelectAction → Processing → DispensingCash, with each state handling only valid transitions.

items: State pattern: ATM has distinct states with valid operations per state
Card: cardNumber, expiryDate, accountId
Account: accountId, balance, accountType
BankServer: verifyPin(), getBalance(), debit() — external system interface
CashDispenser: tracks available cash, dispense(amount)
CardReader: reads card data
Security: PIN verification through BankServer, never store PIN locally

answer_sections.content: An ATM is a good example of the State design pattern. The ATM has distinct states: Idle, CardInserted, Authenticated, Dispensing, OutOfService. Each state allows only specific operations — in Idle state you can only insert a card; trying to enter a PIN does nothing. The State pattern makes this clean: each ATMState implementation handles the valid transitions and ignores invalid operations. Key entities: Card (just a number and expiry), Account (balance and type), CashDispenser (tracks and dispenses cash), BankServer (external bank system for PIN verification and balance queries). Security-critical design: never store or log the PIN anywhere in the ATM — only send it to BankServer for verification and immediately discard it.

sections.title: ATM System Architecture Overview
sections.content: An ATM system is a **state-driven transaction processor** that coordinates hardware components (card reader, cash dispenser, keypad) with backend bank services. The design centers on the **State pattern** because an ATM behaves completely differently depending on its current phase—you can't withdraw cash before authentication, and you can't authenticate without a card inserted. The **ATM class** acts as a Singleton controller (one logical ATM per machine) that delegates all operations to its **currentState** object. Hardware components like **CashDispenser** and **CardReader** are abstracted as separate classes so the core logic doesn't know whether it's talking to physical hardware or test stubs. The **BankServer** interface represents the external banking system—account verification, balance checks, and transaction posting happen through this boundary. This separation keeps your ATM logic testable without needing a real bank backend. Each **Account** has a type (Savings, Checking) that determines withdrawal limits, and the **Card** object carries identification but never stores sensitive data like PINs. The state machine ensures security: once authentication fails three times, the system ejects the card and locks the account, preventing brute-force PIN attacks.

sections.title: Core ATM System Classes
Key Design Points
content: **State Pattern**: Each ATM state (IdleState, CardInsertedState, AuthenticatedState) implements ATMState and handles only valid operations for that phase, throwing exceptions for invalid actions
**Singleton ATM**: One ATM instance per machine ensures centralized state management and prevents multiple concurrent sessions on the same hardware
**Hardware Abstraction**: CashDispenser, CardReader, and ScreenDisplay are separate classes so core logic doesn't depend on physical hardware details
**BankServer Interface**: External bank communication is abstracted behind an interface, making the system testable with mock implementations without needing real banking infrastructure
**Security by Design**: PIN is verified immediately and discarded (never stored), failed attempts increment a counter leading to card lockout after 3 tries
**Account Types**: Different account types (Savings vs Checking) have different withdrawal limits enforced through Strategy pattern on Account.type
**Audit Trail**: Every state transition and transaction is logged with timestamp, card number, and action for compliance and debugging

sections.title: How to Answer in Interview
sections.content: I'd design the ATM system around a state machine because an ATM's behavior changes completely based on where you are in the transaction flow. The main class is ATM, which I'd make a Singleton since there's one logical controller per machine. It holds a currentState object that implements the ATMState interface. That interface defines all possible operations like insertCard, enterPIN, selectWithdrawal, and dispenseCash. Each concrete state class, like IdleState or AuthenticatedState, implements only the transitions that make sense for that phase. If you try to withdraw cash before authenticating, the state throws an exception or does nothing. I'd separate hardware concerns into their own classes. CashDispenser manages the physical bills and tracks how many of each denomination are available. CardReader handles card insertion and ejection. This separation means the core ATM logic doesn't know if it's talking to real hardware or test mocks, which makes unit testing way easier. The BankServer interface represents the external banking system. All account verification, balance checks, and transaction posting go through this boundary. In a real system, this would make HTTPS calls to the bank's API, but in tests you'd inject a stub. For security, the PIN is never stored anywhere. When you enter it, the ATM immediately calls bankServer.verifyPIN and then discards the PIN string. If verification fails three times, the system ejects the card and locks the account. I'd also add a session timeout so if you walk away mid-transaction, the ATM automatically ejects your card after 30 seconds of inactivity. One thing interviewers often miss in candidate answers is the audit trail. Every transaction and state change should be logged with a timestamp and card number for compliance. That's just a simple logger call in each state transition, but it's critical for real financial systems.

questions.question: How do you model the State pattern for an ATM?

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of State pattern mechanics—how state objects collaborate and transition control flow
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using enum or switch statements instead of polymorphic state objects, which creates a maintenance nightmare as states grow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that each state object can hold state-specific data (like failed PIN attempts in AuthenticatedState) and demonstrate setState() call with concrete state names

questions.direct_answer: The State pattern uses an ATMState interface defining all operations (insertCard, enterPIN, withdraw, etc.). Each concrete state class implements only valid transitions for that phase; invalid operations throw IllegalStateException or do nothing. The ATM object holds a currentState reference and delegates every user action to currentState.operation(), and states call atm.setState() to transition.

answer_sections.content: The State pattern encapsulates what operations are valid in each ATM state. The ATMState interface declares all possible user actions. Each concrete state implements only the valid ones — IdleState responds to insertCard(), ignores enterPin(). CardInsertedState responds to enterPin(), ignores insertCard(). This eliminates the complex nested conditionals you'd otherwise need: 'if currentState is IDLE and action is INSERT_CARD, then...' The ATM class is clean: it just delegates to currentState.performAction(). State transitions happen inside state objects — IdleState.insertCard() calls atm.setState(new CardInsertedState()). New states can be added without modifying existing state classes.

sections.title: State Pattern Implementation for ATM
sections.content: The **State pattern** eliminates complex conditional logic by turning each ATM phase into a separate object. Instead of one giant ATM class with nested if-else checks on currentPhase, you create an **ATMState interface** with methods for every possible user action: insertCard(), enterPIN(), selectWithdrawal(), dispenseCash(), ejectCard(). Each concrete state like **IdleState** or **AuthenticatedState** implements this interface but only provides real behavior for operations valid in that state. Invalid operations either throw **IllegalStateException** ("Can't withdraw without authentication") or silently do nothing, depending on UX requirements. The **ATM context object** holds a currentState reference and delegates every operation to it: when a user calls atm.withdraw(200), the ATM just calls currentState.selectWithdrawal(this, 200). The magic is in **state transitions**: inside each state method, after performing its logic, the state calls atm.setState(new NextState()) to move the machine forward. For example, when PIN verification succeeds in CardInsertedState, it calls atm.setState(new AuthenticatedState(account)) to unlock withdrawal operations. This design is **self-documenting**—reading the state classes tells you exactly what's allowed at each phase—and it's **open for extension**: adding a new state (like MaintenanceState) doesn't require touching existing state code.

sections.title: State Pattern Implementation
Key Implementation Points
content: **ATMState Interface**: Defines all possible operations as methods—every state must implement every method, even if just to reject it
**Concrete State Classes**: Each state (IdleState, CardInsertedState, AuthenticatedState, DispensingCashState) implements ATMState with logic specific to that phase
**Invalid Operations**: Methods not valid for a state either throw IllegalStateException with a clear message or print an error and do nothing—never crash silently
**State Transitions**: Each state calls atm.setState(new NextState()) after completing its logic to move the machine forward—transitions are explicit and localized
**State-Specific Data**: States can hold their own fields like failedAttempts in CardInsertedState, which resets when transitioning out
**Context Reference**: Every state method receives the ATM context object so it can access shared data (currentCard, currentAccount) and trigger transitions
**No Enums or Switches**: The pattern eliminates if-else chains on currentPhase by using polymorphism—adding a new state means adding a new class, not modifying existing code

sections.title: How to Answer in Interview
sections.content: I'd start with an ATMState interface that defines all possible user operations: insertCard, enterPIN, selectWithdrawal, dispenseCash, and ejectCard. Every operation takes the ATM context object as a parameter so states can access shared data and trigger state transitions. Then I'd create a concrete class for each ATM phase. IdleState only allows insertCard—when you call that method, it stores the card in the ATM context and calls atm.setState with a new CardInsertedState instance to transition forward. All the other methods in IdleState throw IllegalStateException because you can't enter a PIN or withdraw money when no card is inserted. CardInsertedState handles PIN entry. It keeps a failedAttempts counter as an instance field. When enterPIN is called, it asks the BankServer to verify the PIN. If verification succeeds, it transitions to AuthenticatedState by calling atm.setState. If it fails, it increments failedAttempts. After three failures, it ejects the card and transitions back to IdleState. The key thing is each state only implements what makes sense for that phase. AuthenticatedState allows selectWithdrawal but rejects insertCard because there's already a card in. When you select a withdrawal amount, AuthenticatedState transitions to DispensingCashState, which coordinates with the CashDispenser to physically output bills. One thing freshers miss is that states can hold data specific to that phase. The failedAttempts counter only exists in CardInsertedState and resets when you transition out. You don't need a global attempt counter that persists across sessions. The ATM context object just holds a currentState reference and delegates everything to it. When you call atm.withdraw, the ATM doesn't have any logic—it just calls currentState.selectWithdrawal. That's the whole point of the pattern: the ATM class stays simple, and all the phase-specific behavior lives in the state objects.

questions.question: How does the cash dispensing algorithm work in your ATM design?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can implement a classic greedy algorithm in a real-world constraint problem (limited bill inventory, exact change requirement)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to check if exact change is possible before starting dispensing—you can't give back bills once started
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the edge case where greedy fails (e.g., have 3×$20 but need $50) and explain you'd need backtracking or reject the transaction if exact change isn't possible

questions.direct_answer: The CashDispenser uses a greedy algorithm: it maintains a sorted map of denomination to count (e.g., 100→50 bills, 50→100 bills). For a withdrawal amount, iterate denominations from largest to smallest. For each denomination, dispense min(requestedAmount / denomination, availableCount) bills, subtract from both amount and inventory, repeat until amount reaches zero or no bills remain.

answer_sections.content: The cash dispensing algorithm is a greedy problem: use the fewest bills possible. I store denominations in a TreeMap (sorted by denomination size). Iterating in descending order — 500, 200, 100, 50, 20, 10 — for each denomination I calculate how many I can use: minimum of remaining/denomination and how many I have. This greedy approach gives the minimum number of bills for most currency systems. I check that the full amount can be dispensed; if remaining > 0 after trying all denominations, the requested amount can't be made with available bills (e.g., requesting 30 when only 50-rupee notes available). This is also where I need atomicity — I shouldn't update the physical cash count until the transaction is confirmed.

follow_up_questions: Does the greedy algorithm always give the minimum number of bills? When does it fail?
How do you handle the atomicity of updating cash levels and debiting the account?

beats.text: CashDispenser holds a TreeMap of denomination to count. To dispense an amount, iterate denominations from largest to smallest, using as many of each as possible without exceeding the remaining amount.

items: TreeMap in descending order: 500, 200, 100, 50, 20, 10
For each denomination: count = min(remaining divided by denomination, available count)
Subtract count times denomination from remaining, record the count used
After all denominations: if remaining is greater than 0, throw InsufficientCashException

beats.text: Dispensing 730 with denominations 500, 200, 100, 50: take one 500 (remaining 230), one 200 (remaining 30), zero 100s (can't use), zero 50s (can't use). Result: remaining is 30 and can't be dispensed — the exception fires.

sharp edge: greedy gives minimum bills for standard currency systems, but it doesn't work for arbitrary denomination sets. For example, with denominations 6 and 9, greedy fails for amount 12. In an interview, acknowledging this edge case shows algorithmic depth.

speakable_v2.cap: Greedy descending order, TreeMap for denomination storage, InsufficientCashException if amount can't be made. Mention the greedy failure case — it's the detail that impresses.

sections.title: Cash Dispensing Algorithm Design
sections.content: The **CashDispenser** solves a classic **change-making problem** with limited inventory: given an amount like $370 and available denominations ($100, $50, $20, $10), output the minimum number of bills. The **greedy approach** works here because standard ATM denominations form a **canonical coin system**—larger denominations are always multiples or near-multiples of smaller ones, so taking the largest bill first always leads to an optimal solution. The algorithm maintains a **TreeMap<Integer, Integer>** (denomination → count) sorted in descending order. For each denomination, dispense as many bills as possible without exceeding the remaining amount: if you need $370 and have $100 bills, dispense 3, leaving $70. Then try $50 (can't use any), then $20 (use 3, leaving $10), then $10 (use 1, done). The **critical constraint** is exact change: if after processing all denominations the remaining amount isn't zero, the transaction must fail—you can't dispense $370 if you only have $100 bills. Before dispensing, you should **validate feasibility**: can this amount be constructed with available bills? A simple check is if amount % smallestDenomination != 0, reject immediately. The algorithm updates inventory by decrementing counts as it dispenses, and it should be **transactional**: if dispensing fails mid-way (e.g., a bill jams), roll back the inventory changes so the ATM state stays consistent.

sections.title: Cash Dispensing Algorithm Implementation
Algorithm Key Points
content: **Greedy Strategy**: Always dispense the largest denomination first—works optimally for standard ATM bills ($100, $50, $20, $10, $5) because they form a canonical system
**Inventory Constraint**: Can't dispense more bills of a denomination than available—use Math.min(needed, available) to cap at inventory
**Exact Change Validation**: Before starting, check if the amount can be constructed with available bills—reject if amount % smallestDenomination != 0 or if total inventory is less than amount
**Transactional Rollback**: If dispensing fails partway through (remaining > 0 after all denominations), restore the inventory to its pre-attempt state
**TreeMap Descending Order**: Use TreeMap with Comparator.reverseOrder() so iterating processes largest denominations first without manual sorting
**Edge Case—Greedy Failure**: If inventory is {$20→3} and amount is $50, greedy can't solve it even though total is $60—need backtracking or reject transaction
**Reload Operation**: Support reloading the ATM by merging new bill counts into existing inventory without replacing denominations

sections.title: How to Answer in Interview
sections.content: I'd use a greedy algorithm for cash dispensing because ATM denominations like $100, $50, $20, and $10 form what's called a canonical coin system. That means always taking the largest bill first gives you the optimal solution—the fewest total bills. The CashDispenser class holds a TreeMap that maps denomination to count, sorted in descending order so when I iterate, I naturally process largest bills first. For a withdrawal amount like $370, I start with $100 bills. I calculate how many I'd ideally use, which is 370 divided by 100, so 3 bills. But I also check how many $100 bills are actually available in the machine. I take the minimum of those two numbers. If I have 50 hundreds in inventory and need 3, I dispense 3. Then I subtract $300 from the remaining amount, leaving $70, and I update the inventory by decrementing the $100 count. Next I move to $50 bills. 70 divided by 50 is 1, but after dispensing one $50 I'd have $20 left, so I actually take zero $50s because I want to minimize bills. Then I try $20s. 70 divided by 20 is 3, and I have plenty of $20s, so I dispense 3 and subtract $60, leaving $10. Finally I dispense one $10 bill and remaining hits zero. The result is a map showing 3×$100, 3×$20, 1×$10. One critical thing is exact change validation. Before I start dispensing, I check if the amount is even possible with the bills I have. The simplest check is whether the amount is a multiple of the smallest denomination. If someone requests $37 and my smallest bill is $10, I reject immediately. I also check if I have enough total cash—sum up denomination times count across all bills and make sure it's at least the requested amount. A trickier edge case is when greedy fails. Imagine I only have three $20 bills and someone requests $50. My total inventory is $60, which is more than $50, but there's no combination of $20s that gives exactly $50. In that case, after iterating all denominations, my remaining amount is still $10, so I have to reject the transaction and roll back any inventory changes I made. That rollback is important—if I already decremented some bill counts, I need to add them back so the ATM state stays consistent.

questions.question: What security considerations are important in your ATM design?

interviewer_intent.testing: Security-aware design thinking—whether you consider threat models (PIN theft, man-in-the-middle, physical tampering) beyond just functional requirements
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only mentioning password encryption but ignoring session management, audit logging, or communication security
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention specific attack vectors (shoulder surfing, card skimming) and how your design mitigates them, plus regulatory compliance (PCI-DSS) requirements

questions.direct_answer: Key security principles: (1) Never store PINs—verify immediately via BankServer and discard, (2) Encrypt all communication with BankServer using TLS, (3) Limit PIN attempts to 3 before locking the card, (4) Session timeout—eject card after 30 seconds of inactivity, (5) Audit trail—log every transaction and state change with timestamp and card number for compliance and fraud detection.

items: PIN: never store in ATM memory beyond the verification call
Bank communication: encrypted channel to BankServer
PIN attempts: ATMState tracks failed attempts, locks card after 3 failures
Session timeout: IdleState set after N seconds of inactivity
Audit log: every transaction logged with timestamp, account, amount
Card retention: ATM can swallow card on repeated failures

answer_sections.content: Security in the ATM design requires several deliberate choices. PIN never gets stored: CardInsertedState receives the PIN from the keypad, immediately sends it to BankServer.verifyPin(), and discards it — it never goes into any log or field. Failed attempt tracking in the state: after 3 wrong PINs, transition to CardLockedState which retains the card. Session timeout: if the AuthenticatedState has no action for 30 seconds, eject the card and return to IdleState. Audit trail: every state transition and every transaction is logged to an immutable audit log — who, when, what amount, success/failure. Communication with the bank server uses encrypted channels and the ATM authenticates to the bank server as well as the user authenticating to the ATM.

What is the two-factor authentication in an ATM (something you have + something you know)?

beats.text: An ATM handles real money and real people's accounts. Security isn't an afterthought — it shapes specific design decisions.

items: PIN never stored: receive it, call BankServer.verifyPin(), discard — never logs, never fields
Failed attempt tracking: CardInsertedState counts failures — card locked after 3 wrong PINs
Session timeout: AuthenticatedState triggers card ejection after N seconds of inactivity
Audit trail: every state transition and transaction logged with timestamp — immutable, never deletable

beats.text: Two-factor auth is built into the ATM design: the card is something you have, the PIN is something you know. Both are required. The ATM hardware handles the card; the BankServer handles PIN verification. Neither alone is sufficient.

candidates miss: the audit trail. A design without an immutable transaction log isn't production-grade for a financial system. Even in an LLD interview, mentioning it shows you think about accountability.

speakable_v2.cap: Never log the PIN, lock after 3 failures, timeout on inactivity, and always audit every transaction. Raise these points proactively — they signal security-conscious design.

sections.title: Security Architecture for ATM Systems
sections.content: ATM security design must address **physical attacks** (card skimming, camera recording PINs), **network attacks** (man-in-the-middle on bank communication), and **logical attacks** (brute-force PIN guessing, session hijacking). The cardinal rule is **never store PINs**—when a user enters a PIN, the ATM immediately sends it to the BankServer for verification and then zeroes out the memory. Even in logs, PINs never appear. All communication with the bank uses **TLS encryption** (Transport Layer Security) with certificate pinning to prevent attackers from intercepting account balances or transaction data. To stop **brute-force attacks**, the system allows only 3 PIN attempts before ejecting the card and locking the account—this counter lives in the CardInsertedState and resets only on successful authentication. **Session timeouts** prevent someone from walking away mid-transaction and leaving their account exposed: after 30 seconds of inactivity, the ATM automatically ejects the card and resets to IdleState. Every operation must leave an **audit trail**: who (card number, masked to last 4 digits in logs), what (withdraw $200), when (ISO 8601 timestamp), and result (success or failure reason). This log is tamper-evident—append-only, ideally stored on a write-once medium. For **physical security**, the card reader should have anti-skimming hardware, and the keypad should have a PIN pad shield to prevent cameras from capturing entries. The cash dispenser is locked in a vault accessible only with dual-key authorization during maintenance.

sections.title: Security-Aware ATM Implementation
Security Design Key Points
content: **No PIN Storage**: PIN is verified immediately via BankServer and then nulled out—never stored in memory, logs, or database
**TLS Encryption**: All BankServer communication uses HTTPS with TLS 1.3 and certificate pinning to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks on account data
**PIN Attempt Limiting**: Lock card after 3 failed PIN attempts—counter lives in state object and triggers bankServer.lockCard() before ejecting
**Session Timeout**: After 30 seconds of inactivity, automatically eject card and reset to IdleState—prevents unauthorized access if user walks away
**Audit Trail**: Log every operation (PIN attempt, withdrawal, ejection) with timestamp and masked card number (last 4 digits only) for compliance and fraud investigation
**Physical Security**: Anti-skimming hardware on card reader, PIN shield on keypad, dual-key vault for cash dispenser—design assumes ATM is in untrusted physical location
**Regulatory Compliance**: PCI-DSS requires no cleartext PIN storage, encrypted transmission, and tamper-evident logging—design must support audits

sections.title: How to Answer in Interview
sections.content: Security is critical in ATM design because you're handling money and sensitive data in a physically exposed location. The first principle is never store PINs anywhere. When the user enters a PIN, my code immediately calls bankServer.verifyPIN and then sets the PIN variable to null. I'd even suggest garbage collection, though that's not guaranteed in Java. The point is the PIN should exist in memory for the absolute minimum time. All communication with the BankServer happens over HTTPS with TLS encryption. In production, I'd use certificate pinning so even if an attacker intercepts the network, they can't decrypt the account balance or transaction data without the exact bank certificate. To prevent brute-force PIN guessing, I limit attempts to 3. The CardInsertedState object holds a failedAttempts counter. On the third failure, the ATM calls bankServer.lockCard to tell the bank to disable that card, then ejects it. The user can't try again without calling the bank. Session timeout is another layer. If the user walks away after authentication, their account is exposed until they come back. So I start a 30-second timer when they authenticate. Every user action, like pressing a button or selecting an amount, resets the timer. If it expires, the ATM automatically ejects the card and goes back to IdleState. This protects against someone walking away mid-transaction. Every operation must be logged for audits. I'd have an AuditLogger class that writes entries with a timestamp, action type, and masked card number. The log only shows the last 4 digits of the card for privacy. In production, this log would go to append-only storage so attackers can't delete their tracks. For physical security, I'd mention anti-skimming devices on the card reader and a PIN shield over the keypad to block cameras. The cash dispenser sits in a locked vault that requires two keys to open during maintenance. One thing that stands out is mentioning PCI-DSS compliance. The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard requires all these measures—no plaintext PINs, encrypted transmission, tamper-evident logs. Saying you designed with compliance in mind shows you understand real-world constraints beyond just coding.

questions.question: What design patterns did you use in the ATM design and why?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can articulate why each pattern fits the problem—not just name-dropping but explaining the design trade-off each pattern solves
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing patterns without justification or using patterns unnecessarily (e.g., Factory when direct instantiation is simpler)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention a pattern you deliberately avoided and why (e.g., didn't use Observer because ATM state changes are synchronous, not event-driven)

questions.direct_answer: Key patterns: (1) State pattern for clean state machine (Idle, CardInserted, Authenticated, DispensingCash states), (2) Singleton for ATM controller (one instance per machine), (3) Strategy pattern for account types (Savings vs Checking have different withdrawal limits), (4) Command pattern for each ATM action (enables undo and audit logging), (5) Facade pattern where ATM class hides CashDispenser, CardReader, BankServer complexity from user interaction layer.

answer_sections.content: I applied: State pattern for ATM state machine — it's the most natural fit for systems with explicit lifecycle states and state-dependent behavior. Singleton for ATM itself — one ATM controller per machine. Strategy for withdrawal limits — SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount have different daily withdrawal limits, encapsulated in a WithdrawalLimitStrategy. Facade: the ATM class provides a simple interface (insertCard, enterPin, withdraw) that hides the complexity of CardReader, BankServer, CashDispenser underneath. Command pattern could be applied to record each user action as a Command object for audit trails and potential undo. Each pattern solves a specific design challenge rather than being applied for its own sake.

speakable_v2.hook: Naming patterns with reasons — not just listing them — is the difference between a memorized answer and a design answer.

beats.text: The ATM design applies multiple patterns, and each one earns its place by solving a specific problem. Here's the full set with the problem each one solves.

groups.heading: State
groups.text: ATM has distinct lifecycle states with state-dependent valid operations. State pattern encapsulates this without nested conditionals.

groups.heading: Singleton
groups.text: One ATM controller per machine. Multiple instances would cause inconsistent state.

groups.heading: Strategy — withdrawal limits
groups.text: Savings and Current accounts have different daily withdrawal limits. WithdrawalLimitStrategy encapsulates this so Account doesn't need branches.

groups.heading: Facade
groups.text: The ATM class provides a simple interface (insertCard, enterPin, withdraw) that hides CardReader, BankServer, and CashDispenser complexity from the user interaction layer.

groups.heading: Command
groups.text: Each ATM action can be wrapped in a Command object for the audit trail. Commands are immutable records of what happened — they support replay for reconciliation.

beats.text: non-obvious: Facade is often overlooked in ATM design. The ATM class itself is a Facade — it simplifies a complex subsystem (card reading, bank communication, cash counting) into a clean interface. Naming it makes you sound like you understand the pattern, not just the plumbing.

speakable_v2.cap: State for lifecycle, Singleton for the controller, Strategy for limits, Facade for simplifying subsystems, Command for audit. Every pattern has a reason — know the reason.

sections.title: Design Pattern Selection for ATM System
sections.content: Design patterns in an ATM system solve specific structural and behavioral problems. The **State pattern** is unavoidable because an ATM is fundamentally a state machine—its behavior changes completely based on current phase (idle vs authenticated vs dispensing). Without State, you'd have nested if-else on currentPhase in every method, which becomes unmaintainable. The **Singleton pattern** ensures one ATM controller instance per machine, preventing multiple concurrent sessions that could corrupt state (imagine two users thinking they're both authenticated). The **Strategy pattern** handles account type differences: a SavingsAccount might allow $500 daily withdrawals while a CheckingAccount allows $1000, but both implement the same AccountType interface, so the ATM doesn't need to know which is which. The **Command pattern** wraps each user action (WithdrawCommand, BalanceInquiryCommand) as an object with execute() and undo() methods—this enables audit logging (serialize the command) and rollback (if dispensing fails, undo the debit). The **Facade pattern** is implicit: the ATM class presents a simple interface (insertCard, withdraw, ejectCard) that hides the complexity of coordinating CashDispenser, CardReader, BankServer, and state transitions. One pattern you **don't** need is Observer—ATM state changes are synchronous and single-threaded, not asynchronous events requiring publish-subscribe. Overusing patterns here would add complexity without benefit.

sections.title: Pattern Usage in ATM Design
Pattern Selection Key Points
content: **State Pattern**: Eliminates conditional logic by making each phase (Idle, Authenticated, Dispensing) a separate class—cleanly models ATM state machine with explicit transitions
**Singleton Pattern**: One ATM instance per machine prevents concurrent sessions corrupting shared state like currentCard and currentAccount
**Strategy Pattern**: Different account types (Savings, Checking, Credit) have different withdrawal limits—strategy encapsulates this variation without ATM needing to know account internals
**Command Pattern**: Each user action is a Command object with execute, undo, and getAuditLog methods—enables rollback on failure and structured audit trail
**Facade Pattern**: ATM class provides simple methods (insertCard, withdraw, ejectCard) that hide the orchestration of multiple subsystems (CashDispenser, BankServer, state transitions)
**Avoided Observer Pattern**: ATM operations are synchronous and single-threaded—no need for publish-subscribe or asynchronous event handling, which would add unnecessary complexity
**Pattern Discipline**: Only use patterns that solve a real problem in your design—overusing patterns (e.g., Factory for every object creation) makes code harder to understand, not easier

sections.title: How to Answer in Interview
sections.content: I chose patterns based on the specific problems each solves. The State pattern is essential because an ATM is a state machine. Its behavior is completely different depending on whether you're in IdleState, CardInsertedState, or AuthenticatedState. Without State, I'd have nested if statements checking currentPhase in every method, which gets messy fast. With State, each phase is a separate class that only implements valid operations for that context. The Singleton pattern ensures there's exactly one ATM controller per machine. If you allowed multiple ATM instances, two users could both think they're authenticated at the same time, corrupting the shared currentAccount field. Singleton prevents that by making the constructor private and providing a synchronized getInstance method. For account types, I used the Strategy pattern. A SavingsAccount might have a $500 daily withdrawal limit, while a CheckingAccount allows $1000. Both implement the WithdrawalStrategy interface with a canWithdraw method. The ATM doesn't need to know which account type it's dealing with—it just calls account.canWithdraw and the strategy object handles the rules. That's way cleaner than having a switch statement on account type. The Command pattern wraps each user action like withdraw or balance inquiry as an object with execute, undo, and getAuditLog methods. This is useful for two reasons. First, if dispensing cash fails halfway through, I can call undo on the WithdrawCommand to credit the account back. Second, every command can serialize itself to an audit log by returning a string with the action details. That's much better than scattering logging calls throughout the code. The Facade pattern is implicit in the ATM class itself. From the user's perspective, they just call atm.withdraw and it works. Behind the scenes, the ATM is coordinating with the state object, the CashDispenser, the BankServer, and the audit logger. But all that complexity is hidden behind a simple public interface. One pattern I deliberately avoided is Observer. You might think state transitions should trigger events, but ATM operations are synchronous. When you insert a card, the state changes immediately in the same thread. There's no need for asynchronous publish-subscribe machinery. Adding Observer would just make the code harder to follow without any real benefit. The key is to use patterns only when they solve a concrete problem in your design, not just because you know them.
